title: "Impact of COVID-19 Waves on Normal and Abnormal Stock Returns: Evidence from the Indian Stock Market"
affiliations: Delhi Technological University, New Delhi, Delhi Technological University, New Delhi and Delhi Technological University, New Delhi

detail.title: "Impact of COVID-19 Waves on Normal and Abnormal Stock Returns: Evidence from the Indian Stock Market"
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on Indian stock market returns using an event-study framework. Employing daily data from NIFTY 50 and sectoral indices, abnormal returns were computed for both the first and second pandemic waves, followed by a paired t-test and regression analysis as a measure of market uncertainty. Results reveal that market reactions were stronger and more negative during the first wave, whereas the second wave reflected greater investor adaptation and selective sectoral resilience. The findings contribute to understanding market efficiency and behavioral responses during systemic crises.

title: The Causal Impact of Children? Rethinking The Identification and Estimation of Child Penalties

detail.title: The Causal Impact of Children? Rethinking The Identification and Estimation of Child Penalties
detail.abstract: A fast-growing literature estimates child penalties-the impact of parenthood on the labor market outcomes of mothers relative to fathers-using event study design. This paper clarifies the identification assumption underlying the most commonly used specification with event time, year, and age fixed effects, and shows that this approach is prone to bias in the presence of heterogeneity by age and calendar year, even under valid identification. I then propose an unbiased estimator, using the same identification framework. Applied to French administrative data, my estimates for mothers are 27% smaller than those using the standard approach. The paper also discusses identification under an alternative parallel trend assumption, that is, when controlling for individual unobserved heterogeneity, and highlights key trade-offs in defining counterfactuals, as one cannot simultaneously absorb individual heterogeneity, age, age at birth, and event time. I provide a framework to build an estimator step-by-step, which is easily adaptable depending on which comparisons researchers assess most appropriate. Finally, I document substantial heterogeneity by age at childbirth for both mothers and fathers. By eight years after the birth of their first child, mothers aged 20-25 at birth lose 50% compared to their counterfactual earnings, compared to 12-20% for older mothers. Fathers aged 20-25 at first birth earn on average 26% less eight years later, while effects for older fathers are close to zero. These findings have important implications for both policy and applied research using event study designs to estimate the causal impact of children.

title: Infrastructural Finance in Education and Health in West Bengal

detail.title: Infrastructural Finance in Education and Health in West Bengal
detail.abstract: The focus of this paper is social sector development through social infrastructure in education and health. Since 1990, when the first Human Development Report was published, education (access to knowledge, as measured by the adult literacy rate and the combined gross enrolment ratio in education, HDI 2007) and health (a long and healthy life, as measured by life expectancy at birth, HDI 2007) along with income ( standard of living measured by purchasing power parity) became the three pillars of Human Development Index for the countries in the world. But here we concentrate only on the first two aspects. The State of West Bengal in India as per 2001 Census, has a literacy rate of about 69 per cent and occupies the 19th position among the Indian states and union territories. The literacy rate in the state has always been higher than the all-India average (65 per cent approx.). Although the literacy rate in West Bengal has increased from 48.6 per cent in 1981 to 57.7 per cent in 1991 and to 69.2 per cent in 2001(Census,2001) the total number of literates were 47,196,401 ( Census,2001) with a total population of 80,000,000 approx. It was the most densely populated state in the country in 2001.The gross enrolment for 6-11 year age-group was 85.60 per cent whereas the net enrolment was only 40.2 per cent in 1997-98. Various sociological and economic factors can be credited for a high population density which makes provision of basic infrastructure such as health and education a very challenging task. On the other hand, health infrastructure, which is an important indicator to understand the healthcare delivery provisions and mechanisms in a state indicates the priority accorded to creating the infrastructure in public and private sectors through investments. West Bengal ranks third in India with respect to infant mortality rates but still the average level of nutrition of a child is below national average. The public health system here bears an exceptionally large burden, because in addition to the high demographic pressure in the state, the bulk of curative services are in public hands, such as 76 per cent of the health institutes in West Bengal which are run by the government. While the state finances and manages the basic health infrastructure, the private sector predominantly provides the ambulatory care services. Although the last 50 years, have seen a paradigm shift in country's health care infrastructure from a mainly urban and clinic based to the creation of preventive and rehabilitative services by building up the primary, secondary and tertiary care institutions but still the total infrastructure in terms of population growth is far below the required level. Since Government is already over-burdened with lots of financial responsibilities, we need to look for other alternatives and interventions like private sector but definitely with some definite regulatory measures. Can a part of the social sector be truly left in private hands for the betterment?

title: Price-Match Guarantees and Investment Incentives
affiliations: University of Alabama and Alfaisal University

detail.title: Price-Match Guarantees and Investment Incentives

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no competing interests to declare that are relevant to the content of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: We did not receive funding from any source.

detail.abstract: We consider duopoly sequential price competition between a low-cost online firm and a highcost brick-and-mortar firm that decides whether to price-match the low-cost rival. We study how price-match guarantees affect the incentives of both firms to invest in cost reduction and quality enhancement. We find that price-match guarantees in our model weaken these incentives in most cases. Our research reveals more reasons to suspect that seemingly procompetitive price-matching by many offline rivals to online sellers may have hidden social costs.

title: A Holistic Framework for Assessing Digital Energy Trading Platforms in Strategic Corridors: The Case of the Russia-Persian Gulf Energy Axis

detail.title: A Holistic Framework for Assessing Digital Energy Trading Platforms in Strategic Corridors: The Case of the Russia-Persian Gulf Energy Axis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This article is essential reading for scholars, policymakers, and energy market professionals navigating the complex intersection of digital innovation and geopolitics. If you are engaged with any of the following critical questions, this research offers novel insights and a practical framework: · For Researchers: Are you developing assessment tools for digital platforms in strategic sectors? The DESTRICS framework provides a pioneering six-dimensional model that integrates technological, economic, governance, geopolitical, organizational, and environmental factors—moving beyond siloed analysis. · For Energy Analysts & Policymakers: Do you seek to understand why technically feasible digital projects in high-stakes energy corridors often fail? Our case study of the Russia-Persian Gulf axis reveals the "trust deficit paradox": strong techno-economic drivers are systematically neutralized by governance gaps and geopolitical rivalry. We offer a actionable, phased pathway for implementation centered on "mini-lateral" trust-building. · For Scholars of International Relations & Digital Governance: How do digital technologies amplify, rather than transcend, sovereignty anxieties and institutional weaknesses? This article challenges technological determinism, arguing that in strategic contexts, institutional innovation is more critical than technical deployment. · For Professionals in Finance & International Trade: Concerned about sanctions vulnerability and seeking resilient transaction channels? The analysis delves into practical alternatives, including BRICS financial infrastructure and tokenized asset settlements, directly addressing core risk factors. · Unique Contribution: This article synthesizes frequently disconnected literatures on digital platforms, energy geopolitics, and assessment models. It uniquely incorporates vital Russian academic perspectives, offering a more balanced view essential for understanding one of the world's most critical energy corridors. In short, this article provides not just a diagnosis, but a new analytical toolkit and a realistic roadmap for anyone involved in the digital transformation of strategic global trade.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This article is based on a literature review and does not involve any studies with human participants or animals performed by the author.

detail.abstract: The digital transformation of global energy markets intersects with strategic geopolitical realities in complex ways, particularly within vital energy corridors where national security, economic interests, and technological capabilities converge. This article develops and presents the DESTRICS framework (Digital Energy Strategic Trade Corridor Platform Assessment Framework), a comprehensive, six-dimensional analytical tool specifically designed to assess the feasibility, design, and implementation challenges of digital energy trading platforms in geopolitically sensitive corridors. Focusing on the Russia-Persian Gulf energy axis-which collectively governs nearly 40% of global hydrocarbon exports and represents a nexus of both cooperation and competition-this research transcends conventional techno-economic analyses by integrating critical dimensions of transnational governance, geopolitical risk calculus, institutional trust architectures, and socio-organizational readiness. Application of the DESTRICS framework to the Russia-Persian Gulf corridor reveals a fundamental structural paradox: despite strong technical feasibility and compelling economic incentives for digital integration, these positive factors are systematically neutralized by profound governance deficits and entrenched geopolitical rivalries. Our multidimensional assessment identifies a critical "trust gap" as the primary implementation bottleneck, with governance and geopolitical dimensions scoring alarmingly low (1.8 and 2.1 respectively on a 5point readiness scale), while technical and economic dimensions demonstrate significantly higher preparedness (3.2 and 4.1 respectively). This finding challenges prevalent narratives of technological determinism in energy sector digitalization and underscores the primacy of political and institutional factors in strategic corridor contexts. The analysis further demonstrates how technology, rather than transcending political constraints as often assumed, frequently amplifies existing institutional weaknesses and sovereignty anxieties. Consequently, platform design must be fundamentally reconceptualized as an exercise in innovative institutional architecture rather than merely technical implementation. This research contributes both theoretically and practically by: (1) developing a novel assessment framework tailored to strategic energy corridors; (2) providing empirical analysis of the Russia-Persian Gulf case with integrated Russian academic perspectives; (3) proposing an innovative, phased implementation pathway centered on "mini-lateral" trust-building initiatives; and (4) identifying new strategic roles for geographically pivotal states as neutral hosts for digital facilitation entities.

title: The Mathematical Collapse of Cointegration and Error-Correction Models

detail.title: The Mathematical Collapse of Cointegration and Error-Correction Models
detail.abstract: We show that, in the random-walk case, cointegration implies that the error is a constant almost surely. Consequently, cointegration and the ECM collapse. Also, under general assumptions, they collapse almost surely.

title: The Knowledge Ledger: Who Controls Discovery in AI-Mediated Markets

detail.title: The Knowledge Ledger: Who Controls Discovery in AI-Mediated Markets
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems increasingly mediate discovery, comparison, and early-stage decision-making across industries. Yet most industrial knowledge remains fragmented, temporally ambiguous, and structurally unreadable by machines. This paper argues that the primary constraint on effective AI-assisted decision-making is not model capability, but the absence of persistent, time-aware, provenance-based knowledge infrastructure at the industry level. Drawing on the literature on digital timestamping, platform economics, and trust governance, the paper introduces the concept of a Knowledge Ledger: a system for recording industrial capability as an accumulative, time-indexed, and attributable record rather than as static or promotional information. The paper contends that without such infrastructure, control over industrial discovery will default to AI intermediaries and hyperscale platforms, reshaping visibility, competition, and market power. A live industry platform is referenced as an applied instantiation of this framework.

title: Machine Learning for Earnings Forecasting -US and International Evidence
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, Singapore Management University - School of Accountancy and Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto

detail.title: Machine Learning for Earnings Forecasting -US and International Evidence
detail.abstract: This study offers the first large-scale evaluation of various earnings forecasting models, including machine learning (ML) methods, across a sample of US and international firms over multiple horizons. A non-linear tree-based model (Extreme Gradient Boosting or XGBoost) outperforms extant crosssectional forecasting models, a naive random walk model, and penalized linear models. XGBoost is particularly effective in firms for which earnings are more difficult to forecast, such as smaller firms, firms with volatile earnings and high absolute accruals, and loss firms. XGBoost's flexibility in capturing non-linear relationships contributes to its superior performance. Forecasts from XGBoost also display the highest "value relevance" in correlation with future realized returns using two measures: proxies of cash flow news and implied cost of capital (ICC) estimates. We recommend XGBoost for earnings forecasting in both US and international settings.

title: What Drives Corporate Savings
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), , ShanghaiTech University and

detail.title: What Drives Corporate Savings
detail.abstract: We study the determinants of corporate cash holdings by extending the standard q theory of investment with financing frictions and productivity shocks. While existing models predict a low propensity to hold cash, we show that realistic cash holdings arise only when three ingredients are combined: 1.) costly external financing, 2.) persistent productivity shocks, and 3.) contemporaneous productivity shocks. With costly external financing, persistent productivity shocks generate predictable cash flows and investment opportunities, but yield little need for savings since the internally generated cash flows are aligned with the investment needs. Contemporaneous shocks make internally generated cash flows random, inducing firms to hold cash at levels consistent with those observed empirically.

title: Did the Digital Push Last? E-Commerce and Rural Agricultural Earnings in Indonesia During and After COVID-19, Evidence from Sakernas

detail.title: Did the Digital Push Last? E-Commerce and Rural Agricultural Earnings in Indonesia During and After COVID-19, Evidence from Sakernas
detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of e-commerce adoption on earnings and income distribution among rural agricultural employers in Indonesia, both during and after the COVID-19 pandemic. Using microdata from the National Labour Force Survey/Sakernas (2018-2024) and applying probit, OLS, Propensity Score Matching, and quantile regression models, we identify the determinants of adoption and its impact on earnings. Adoption was strongly driven by education, training, and enterprise characteristics, while older age and reliance on unpaid household labor constrained uptake. Results show that e-commerce adopters earned substantially higher than non-adopters (more than 30 percent) both during and after the pandemic, confirming sustained income gains beyond the crisis. Quantile regressions reveal that the lowest-income employers benefited most, with earnings gains exceeding 50 percent at the bottom quantile during the pandemic. Although relative advantages shifted toward higher earners after the pandemic, large and significant effects remained for the lowest-income groups. These findings indicate that e-commerce not only enhances market access but also contributes to improving income distribution. Policy interventions to strengthen digital literacy, rural infrastructure, and financial access are essential to preserve its inclusive role and ensure that vulnerable agricultural employers continue to benefit disproportionately.

detail.title: Meta-t Portfolio Optimization
detail.abstract: We develop a comprehensive theoretical and empirical framework for Meta-t distributions-a flexible class of multivariate distributions that generalize the standard multivariate t-distribution by allowing asset-specific tail parameters. Theoretically, we establish the mathematical foundations including stochastic representations, copula decompositions, moment properties, tail dependence structure, conditional distributions, and stochastic ordering results. We prove consistency and asymptotic normality of estimators and derive closed-form expressions for risk measure sensitivities. Empirically, we analyze daily returns from 25 major US stocks over 20 years (2005-2025), documenting significant tail heterogeneity with degrees of freedom ranging from 3.00 to 6.08. Model comparison via BIC strongly favors Meta-t over standard multivariate t (improvement: 1351.42). Our findings have important implications for portfolio optimization, risk management, and asset allocation.

title: On the Role of Uncertainty in Timing Environmental Policies
affiliations: University of Glasgow, University of Glasgow - Department of Economics, University of Glasgow - Department of Economics and University of Glasgow - Adam Smith Business School

detail.title: On the Role of Uncertainty in Timing Environmental Policies
detail.abstract: We develop an analytical real options framework for the optimal timing of climate policy when both economic cost and stocks of environmental pollutants evolve stochastically and are correlated. By modelling environmental damage as a mean-reverting pollution stock jointly driven with uncertain economic losses, we derive a two-dimensional optimal stopping boundary, moving beyond the singlestate or simplified threshold rules commonly used in earlier work, including Pindyck (2000, 2002). A key theoretical insight is that the option value of waiting depends non-linearly on ecological conditions, reflected in a strictly positive coefficient on pollution in the continuation value, correcting prior simplifications that implied independence from environmental risk. Our analytical characterisation of the exercise boundary shows it is convex and downward-sloping: higher ecological degradation lowers the economic trigger for action. Most importantly, we find that the correlation between state variables governs how rising volatility affects optimal policy timing. When economic and ecological risks are positively correlated, greater volatility accelerates policy adoption, directly contradicting the classical "uncertainty-delay" effect argued by Pindyck, while negative correlation restores the traditional delay incentive. These results underscore that treating uncertainties jointly rather than separately can fundamentally change policy recommendations, with profound implications for climate risk governance and investment under transition and physical risk.

title: A Representation for Partially Observed Structural C-VAR(k) Models

detail.title: A Representation for Partially Observed Structural C-VAR(k) Models
detail.abstract: This paper extends the analysis of partially observed cointegrated systems in Johansen (2019), which underpins recent methods for long-run causal discovery in cointegrated VAR models. We consider a structural C-VAR(k) data-generating process, partition the system into two sets of variables, and derive representations for the cointegration and adjustment matrices of the induced partially observed model fitted to just one of these sets. We show how these representations change relative to the existing literature, where the DGP is a simple C-VAR(1) model with diagonal innovation covariance in its reduced form. Our findings provide a more realistic foundation for procedures that exploit partially observed cointegrated VARs for long-run causal discovery, allowing for richer short-run dynamics and contemporaneous interactions.

title: The Missing Middle: The Disparate Impact of Post-Release Supervision on Returns to Prison and Reconviction
affiliations: Purdue University and University of British Columbia Okanagan

detail.title: The Missing Middle: The Disparate Impact of Post-Release Supervision on Returns to Prison and Reconviction
detail.abstract: In 2011, North Carolina expanded post-release supervision to ≈ 80% of felony releases that previously went unsupervised. Using a regression discontinuity design, we find that 25% of those newly supervised were returned to prison via revocation. This nearly doubled the reincarceration rate one year after release, which remained 35% higher after three years. These revocation effects were racially disparate: Black supervisees were ≈ 40% more likely to be revoked, resulting in 55% more days incarcerated 3 years after initial release. Black supervisees experienced a short-term decline in the new felony conviction rate, consistent with incapacitation. Conversely, the felony conviction rate decreased after 12 months for White supervisees, who were 22% less likely to have a felony reconviction after 3 years. This was offset by a steady increase in the new misdemeanor rate, yielding no net change in the overall reconviction rate. Evidence suggests these effects may have been the result of the discretionary downgrading of new charges for White supervisees.

title: From Frustration to Engagement: Ancillary Services in Queues
affiliations: ShanghaiTech University, University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, University of Western Ontario - Ivey Business School and Southern University of Science and Technology - School of Business

detail.title: From Frustration to Engagement: Ancillary Services in Queues
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Waiting in queues often frustrates customers, erodes profits, and reduces social welfare. Traditional queue management strategies address these issues by reducing congestion or redistributing waiting costs, but overlook opportunities to enhance the waiting experience itself. This paper studies an alternative approach: providing ancillary services that create value during the wait. We explore a fundamental trade-off: while ancillary services improve customer experience, they may also attract more customers and exacerbate congestion. Methodology/results: We develop a game-theoretical queueing model with two customer segments: Type-P customers, who value only the primary service, and Type-A customers, who derive additional utility from a free ancillary service while waiting. Contrary to conventional intuition, ancillary services deliver the greatest benefits precisely when primary service capacity is most constrained. Although ancillary services increase overall congestion, they induce customer self-segmentation: Type-P customers, facing higher delays, do not join the system and are replaced by Type-A customers who value the enriched waiting experience. This substitution effect reshapes the customer mix, enhances throughput, improves customer surplus, and increases profit. We further compare ancillary services to priority queues and show that ancillary services generate higher throughput. They also yield superior profit when Type-A customers constitute a substantial market segment, and deliver higher social welfare when primary service capacity is either highly constrained or abundant. Managerial implications: The results suggest that service providers, especially those operating under capacity constraints, can benefit from implementing ancillary services. By offering value-added experiences during the wait, providers can reshape customer composition, improving throughput and customer welfare without expanding capacity. Compared to priority queues, ancillary services enhance the customer experience without relying on fee-based mechanisms. However, success depends critically on targeting customer segments that value enriched experiences--as seen in Disney's appeal to families or Haidilao's focus on experience-oriented diners.

title: Resilience by Design: A Case Study of Adhocracy and Partnership in Bergamo’s Pandemic Recovery
affiliations: and Bocconi University - Department of Policy Analysis and Public Management

detail.title: Resilience by Design: A Case Study of Adhocracy and Partnership in Bergamo’s Pandemic Recovery
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic revealed the vulnerabilities of traditional bureaucratic governance structures in responding effectively to rapid, large-scale crises. This paper presents a detailed case study of Rinascimento, an innovative urban recovery program launched in Bergamo, Italy-one of the epicenters of the early pandemic. It explores how an adhocratic governance model, characterized by :lexibility, decentralization, and cross-sector collaboration, was employed to mitigate the economic impact of the crisis. The program was implemented through a public-private-nonpro:it partnership involving the Municipality of Bergamo, Intesa Sanpaolo Bank, and CESVI, a local humanitarian NGO. Drawing on collaborative governance and network theories, the Rinascimento initiative combined emergency grants and impact investment loans to support nearly 4,500 small businesses and professionals. The paper analyzes the design and operational mechanisms of the adhocracy, its rapid decision-making capabilities, and its emphasis on real-time learning and adaptation. Empirical evaluation using key performance indicators demonstrates the program's effectiveness in enhancing business resilience, reducing business mortality rates, and fostering economic regeneration. The :indings underscore the potential of adhocratic models in municipal crisis management and offer scalable insights for future governance frameworks addressing systemic shocks.

title: Service Differentiation in Online Healthcare Platforms
affiliations: Sichuan University, University of Houston - Department of Decision & Information Sciences and University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: Service Differentiation in Online Healthcare Platforms
detail.abstract: This study examines a large online healthcare platform that restructured its consultation model from a flat scheme-where all physicians could respond to any patient inquiry-to a tiered service scheme in which access to high-priced consultations is restricted based on physicians' seniority. Leveraging this quasi-experimental policy change and a difference-indifferences design, we find that the introduction of service differentiation significantly reduced provider engagement: physicians subject to the new restrictions were 8.1% less likely to log in and undertook 22.8% fewer patient consultations. Furthermore, while the concreteness of responses remained stable, we observed a 4.6% decline in the matching quality between physician specialty and patient inquiries. To investigate the mechanisms driving these behavioral changes, we conducted a randomized experiment with physician participants. The results reveal that these adverse effects are driven by physicians' negative psychological responses, particularly perceived disrespect, unfairness, and diminished economic expectations. Our study reveals a critical trade-off: while service differentiation aims to enhance efficiency by prioritizing expert resources for more complex and high-paying tasks, it can unintentionally demotivate skilled providers and erode service quality. These results highlight the importance of aligning platform policies not only with demand complexity but also with provider incentives and perceptions.
